connections.feedback: Yes. An unsigned post is a lead, not a fact. Someone who would actually know can tell you quickly whether it is true, and it costs you almost nothing.
Passing it on makes a guess look like news. If it is wrong, many people now believe it, and each of them heard it from you.
No name does not mean false. The post could be right. "Unchecked" and "false" are different, and the way to tell them apart is to ask.
The stakes are low and an official change usually is announced, so waiting is sensible. The cost is that you may be surprised or miss the chance to act, and asking would take a minute.
connections.notes: Reasonable at low stakes; mildly costly if the post turns out to be true.

Fewer reviews are not more honest; they are just fewer. The point is to look at the quality and independence of the reviews, not to flip the rule.
Trying both yourself is direct evidence and avoids the review problem. The cost is the time, and one trial may not show how the app holds up over a term.

connections.feedback: Yes. The claim may be true, but the only support is the seller's own story. Asking how it was measured, or testing it on your own work, turns a promise into evidence you can weigh.
A detailed story feels convincing, but details can be written to persuade. The story comes from the seller and tells you nothing about typical results.
Sellers have a reason to praise a product, but that does not make the claim false. Rejecting it for who said it is as unreliable as accepting it for the same reason.
A user with no sales interest is a better source than the brochure. But it is one person, with their own setup and needs, so it works as a clue and not as a measurement.
connections.notes: Independent but anecdotal; one case may not match your situation.
